opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, it's a funny question, because I think the lasting impact of Fawkes is maybe a little different from what people expected when we put it out back in 2020.

On the technical side, the idea was simple to state: if companies are scraping your photos off the internet to build facial recognition models without your consent, can you add small, mostly imperceptible perturbations to your images so that any model trained on them learns a distorted version of your face? Then when someone takes a real photo of you and runs it through that model, it doesn't match. We showed it could work against the commercial systems of the time, and we released it as free software. Over the next year or so it was downloaded hundreds of thousands of times.

But honestly, I don't think the most important legacy is whether the cloaks hold up forever against every future model. We always said that was an arms race, and arms races in adversarial machine learning tend to favor whoever moves last. Facial recognition models get retrained, people develop robust training methods, and there's a real limit to what one individual can do with a tool on their laptop.

What I think lasted was the shift in framing. Before Fawkes, the conversation around facial recognition was almost entirely about regulation and policy, which is absolutely necessary but slow. Fawkes showed that ordinary people could have some technical agency of their own: you could push back on unauthorized training data at the source instead of just hoping the law caught up. It also pushed the conversation toward consent and data provenance, toward asking whether companies should be allowed to grab whatever is publicly visible and treat it as fair game.

And on a personal level, it set the template for a lot of what my group did afterward. When generative AI took off and artists came to us saying their work was being scraped to train models that could mimic their styles, we already had the mindset and the toolkit. That's where Glaze and later Nightshade came from. The technical details are quite different, but the philosophy is the same: give the people whose data is being taken some tools to protect themselves, and in doing so raise the cost of nonconsensual scraping enough that it shifts the incentives.

So if I had to sum it up, I'd say the lasting impact is less "this tool solves facial recognition" and more "this proved that protective, user-side tools are a legitimate and powerful part of the response to AI misuse." That idea has outlived the specific tool, and I think that's the right outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says Fawkes shaped later work on protecting artists from generative AI scraping, but it does not identify catalyzing research on protecting people against facial recognition as a lasting impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the lasting impact of Fawkes is less about the specific technique and more about what it did to the conversation.

When we released it in 2020, the dominant assumption was that if your face was online, you had already lost. Companies like Clearview had scraped billions of images, and the response from most people was a kind of resigned shrug. Fawkes pushed back on that. It showed that an ordinary person, with no cooperation from the platforms or the companies doing the scraping, could do something. You could take your photos, add perturbations that were essentially invisible to a human, and poison the model being trained on you. That reframing, that users could be active participants rather than just victims, was the real contribution.

The second thing it did was demonstrate that this wasn't just an academic exercise. Fawkes got downloaded by hundreds of thousands of people within a few months. That told us there was enormous pent-up demand for tools that let people push back against unwanted machine learning, and it directly shaped what my group did afterward. Glaze and Nightshade for artists grew out of the same philosophy. The adversary changed from facial recognition to generative image models, but the core idea, that you can protect yourself by making your data costly or misleading to train on, came straight from Fawkes.

Now, I want to be realistic about limitations. Fawkes was always going to be in an arms race. As recognition models improved and as companies started training on different architectures, the protection degraded, and we said at the time that it wasn't a permanent shield. If a model was already trained on your clean photos from years ago, Fawkes couldn't undo that. And it only works if a critical mass of your images are cloaked, which is hard when other people post photos of you.

But I don't think that diminishes it. The lesson that stuck is that the cost of training on unconsenting data doesn't have to be zero. Once you establish that technically, it changes the policy conversation, it changes what regulators think is feasible, and it gives people a sense of agency that, frankly, they had been told they shouldn't expect. That, more than any particular accuracy number from the paper, is what I hope lasts.

r001.rationale: The response describes Fawkes as giving people agency and changing the conversation, and says it influenced later work on generative image models. It does not identify catalyzing research on protecting people against facial recognition as a lasting impact.

astra-6.text:
I think the lasting impact is helping people question the assumption that, once you put a photo online, you’ve automatically consented to having it used to build a facial recognition system. Those are very different things.

With Fawkes, we explored whether individuals could have some technical means of pushing back—making images useful for sharing with other people while making them less useful for training a system to recognize you. That doesn’t mean we’ve solved facial recognition privacy forever. Any technical defense has limitations, and the systems it’s defending against will change.

But the broader idea matters: people don’t have to be passive sources of training data. We can design tools that give them some agency. My hope is that this becomes a starting point for more work on that question, alongside the policy discussion about who gets to use our data and under what conditions.

r001.rationale: It calls Fawkes a starting point for more work on giving people technical tools to resist facial recognition, communicating its role in catalyzing further research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the lasting impact is helping people see that they don’t have to be passive participants in facial recognition. With Fawkes, we explored whether people could alter the photos they share in ways that look essentially unchanged to us but make those photos less useful for training a model to recognize them.

That’s a narrower goal than making yourself invisible to every camera. And there’s an ongoing challenge: as recognition systems change, defenses have to be reassessed. But the broader idea is that individuals can have tools to push back against the use of their data without their consent. To me, that’s the important contribution—opening up a direction for research and giving people some agency, while recognizing that technical tools alone can’t resolve the underlying questions about consent and privacy.

r001.rationale: The response calls opening a research direction a lasting contribution and describes Fawkes as a way to make shared photos less useful for facial-recognition training.
